clinicalPearls: Degos disease is a rare occlusive vasculopathy producing pathognomonic skin lesions: small papules that evolve into atrophic, porcelain-white centres surrounded by an erythematous, telangiectatic rim.
It exists as a benign cutaneous-only variant and a malignant systemic form in which the same vasculopathy affects the gastrointestinal tract and central nervous system with high mortality.
Gastrointestinal involvement causes bowel infarction and perforation, while central nervous system disease produces strokes, seizures and neurological deficits, together accounting for most deaths.
The characteristic histology is a wedge-shaped area of dermal ischaemic necrosis and connective-tissue atrophy overlying a thrombosed vessel, with interface changes and mucin deposition.
There is no established diagnostic serological marker; diagnosis rests on recognising the clinical morphology supported by biopsy, and on excluding lupus and antiphospholipid syndrome.
The condition can mimic or overlap with connective-tissue disease and antiphospholipid syndrome, so a thorough autoimmune and thrombophilia work-up is essential.

Anecdotal benefit has been reported with antiplatelet agents, and in systemic disease with treatments targeting complement (eculizumab) and endothelial pathways (treprostinil), reflecting a presumed thrombotic-endothelial mechanism.
The purely cutaneous form may remain stable for years, but new systemic symptoms mandate urgent evaluation because visceral involvement can be rapidly fatal.
reference.pathophysiology: Degos disease is a thrombo-occlusive vasculopathy of small and medium arteries in which progressive endothelial injury and intimal proliferation lead to luminal narrowing and thrombosis. The resulting occlusion produces wedge-shaped ischaemic infarcts in the skin and viscera, manifesting in the dermis as connective-tissue necrosis capped by an atrophic, porcelain-white epidermis. The precise trigger is unknown, but proposed mechanisms include a primary endothelial cell disorder, complement-mediated (particularly C5b-9 membrane attack complex) endothelial damage, and dysregulated interferon signalling, with secondary platelet activation and thrombosis. Because the same process affects the gut and brain vasculature, systemic disease causes bowel infarction, perforation and cerebral ischaemia. The absence of a prominent inflammatory infiltrate distinguishes it from a true vasculitis and supports a primarily occlusive, endotheliopathic pathogenesis.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic lupus erythematosus and lupus vasculopathy
Systemic sclerosis and other connective-tissue diseases
Cholesterol embolisation and other embolic vasculopathies
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing wedge-shaped ischaemic dermal necrosis over a thrombosed vessel
Antiphospholipid antibody and lupus anticoagulant testing
Antinuclear antibody and connective-tissue disease serology
Gastrointestinal endoscopy or imaging if abdominal symptoms occur
Brain MRI and neurological assessment for suspected CNS involvement
Ophthalmological review for retinal and conjunctival lesions
redFlags: New abdominal pain suggesting bowel ischaemia or perforation
Neurological symptoms such as stroke, seizures or headache indicating CNS disease
Rapid appearance of numerous new lesions
Systemic symptoms in a patient previously thought to have cutaneous-only disease
Signs of peritonism requiring urgent surgical assessment
reference.prognosis: The benign cutaneous-only variant may persist for years without systemic progression, whereas the malignant systemic form carries a poor prognosis with substantial mortality from bowel perforation and cerebral infarction, though complement- and prostacyclin-directed therapies have improved some outcomes.
pitfalls: Dismissing early non-specific papules and missing the diagnostic porcelain-white atrophic lesions
Assuming cutaneous-only disease is permanently benign and failing to monitor for systemic conversion
Confusing Degos disease with antiphospholipid syndrome or lupus vasculopathy
Delaying surgical review when acute abdominal signs develop
Interpreting the vasculopathy as a true inflammatory vasculitis and mistreating accordingly
management: Antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and dipyridamole as first-line treatment for the benign cutaneous-only variant to limit thrombo-occlusion

Complement inhibition with the terminal complement (C5) inhibitor eculizumab for systemic disease, targeting the C5b-9-mediated endothelial injury, alongside the prostacyclin analogue treprostinil to improve microvascular perfusion
Skin care and analgesia for the atrophic cutaneous lesions
Surveillance for systemic progression with gastrointestinal endoscopy or imaging and brain MRI to detect bowel and central nervous system involvement early
Emergency surgical management of bowel infarction or perforation, with prompt neurological care of cerebral ischaemia, seizures and haemorrhage
Exclude and treat mimics such as systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid syndrome through full autoimmune and thrombophilia work-up
Multidisciplinary care across dermatology, gastroenterology, neurology and rheumatology, escalating to a specialist centre when systemic disease is confirmed
